Jaddua
JAD-u-ah
n. (proper, a high priest of the restoration; Hebrew, known)
Hebrew Yadduwa, from yada, to know — known, or one whom God knows. He is the last high priest named in the Old Testament, and the last name in its priestly succession.

Biblical Definition

He sets his seal to the covenant with the chiefs of the people: “Meshezabeel, Zadok, Jaddua” (Nehemiah 10:21). He closes the high-priestly line: “And Joiada begat Jonathan, and Jonathan begat Jaddua” (Nehemiah 12:11). And he stands at the end of the register: “The Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, and Johanan, and Jaddua, were recorded chief of the fathers: also the priests, to the reign of Darius the Persian” (Nehemiah 12:22). With that verse the Old Testament's record of the priesthood stops. Malachi would prophesy, and then four hundred years of silence, and then a priest named Zacharias executing the priest's office before God in the order of his course would be told that his prayer was heard. The last name in the register means known, and the line it closes was waiting for a High Priest after the order of Melchizedek.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the last high priest named in the Old Testament, who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah.

expand to see more

HIGH PRIEST, n. The chief priest among the Hebrews, who alone entered the holy of holies, and that once a year.

SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; a series of persons or things following one another in time or place.

SEAL, v.t. To fasten with a seal; to ratify; to confirm; to settle.

MELCHIZEDEK, n. King of Salem and priest of the most high God, a type of Christ in his priesthood.

SILENCE, n. Absence of sound or noise; stillness; and hence, the cessation of prophecy between the Testaments.

Key Scripture

Nehemiah 10:21 — "Meshezabeel, Zadok, Jaddua,"

Nehemiah 12:11 — "And Joiada begat Jonathan, and Jonathan begat Jaddua."

Nehemiah 12:22 — "The Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, and Johanan, and Jaddua, were recorded chief of the fathers: also the priests, to the reign of Darius the Persian."

Hebrews 7:24 — "But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood."

Modern Corruption

The Old Testament is often read as ending in failure or simply stopping, where its last priestly register closes a line that had been failing for a thousand years and was waiting for a priest who dies no more.

expand to see more

Nehemiah 12:22 is an unremarkable sentence in an unread chapter and it marks the end of something enormous. The line from Aaron is recorded to Jaddua and then stops. Every man in it had one thing in common, which Hebrews states without malice: And they truly were many priests, because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death. A priesthood that must be handed on because its holders keep dying is a priesthood that cannot finally save; the register itself is the argument, generation after generation of men who offered and then were buried.

That is precisely why the next verse in Hebrews lands as it does: But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood. The Old Testament ends its priestly list with a man whose name means known, and four centuries later the true High Priest appears, of whom it is said that he ever liveth to make intercession for them. The register closing is not a failure of the Old Testament but the completion of its argument: here are all the priests, here is where they all stopped, and here is why another was needed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yadduwa (H3037), known; yada (H3045), to know; kohen gadol, high priest; Greek aparabatos (G531), unchangeable.

Hebrew Yadduwa (H3037) — Jaddua; known, or one whom God knows.

Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; the root of the name.

Hebrew kohen (H3548) — a priest; the office his line held from Aaron.

Hebrew chatham (H2856) — to seal; what he did to Nehemiah's covenant.

Greek aparabatos (G531) — unchangeable, not passing to another; Christ's priesthood.

Usage

"“Jonathan begat Jaddua” — the last name in the line."

"“To the reign of Darius the Persian” — where the register stops."

"“This man... hath an unchangeable priesthood” — why another was needed."
